# Executor Framework

The **Executor Framework** separates submitting a task from deciding where and
when it runs. `ExecutorService` adds lifecycle management and `Future` results;
`ScheduledExecutorService` adds delayed and periodic work. An executor can use a
bounded worker pool, but it need not: a virtual-thread-per-task executor creates
a virtual thread for each submitted task.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- choose between `ExecutorService` and `ScheduledExecutorService` based on
  immediate, delayed, or periodic task execution needs;
- distinguish waiting for a `Future` from requesting cancellation, including the
  task’s responsibility to cooperate with interruption; and
- explain why bounded pools and virtual threads need explicit resource and
  lifecycle policies.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 21](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)
JDK or newer and ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to it in the terminal

## The program to inspect

### A single execution-policy story

Imagine one service handling four kinds of independent work: bounded background
jobs, recurring maintenance, many blocking file operations, and a batch whose
results are needed together. The sections below select an executor operation for
each case. They are not interchangeable defaults: the observable ordering,
blocking behaviour, and lifecycle responsibility change with the choice.

### 1. Bounded background jobs and results

A fixed pool limits this example to two concurrent tasks; additional work waits
in its queue. `Future.get()` observes individual results, and the timeout case
demonstrates that waiting and cancellation are separate operations.

`Future.get(timeout, unit)` only limits how long the caller waits; it does not
stop the submitted task. The timeout branch therefore calls `cancel(true)`,
which requests interruption. A task must cooperate with interruption for
cancellation to take effect. Task 4 runs for ten seconds but is waited on for
only three; after cancellation, closing the executor waits for the task to
terminate rather than adding the remaining task duration to the example.

```java
log("Use newFixedThreadPool() to create an executor service using a fixed thread pool");
try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {

    final Runnable runnable = () -> {
        log("Running task 1 (Runnable)");
        sleepForAFewSeconds();
        log("Task 1 completed");
    };
    final Future<?> future1 = executor.submit(runnable);

    final Callable<Long> callable = () -> {
        log("Running task 2 (Callable)");
        sleepForAFewSeconds();
        log("Task 2 completed");
        return 42L;
    };
    final Future<Long> future2 = executor.submit(callable);

    final Future<String> future3 = executor.submit(() -> {
        log("Running task 3 (Runnable+Result)");
        sleepForAFewSeconds();
        log("Task 3 completed");
    }, "Returned once the task completes");

    final Runnable slowRunnable = () -> {
        log("Running (slow) task 4");
        try {
            TimeUnit.SECONDS.sleep(10);
            log("Task 4 completed");
        } catch (final InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            log("Task 4 interrupted");
        }
    };
    final Future<?> future4 = executor.submit(slowRunnable);

    log("Waiting for the futures to finish");

    /* The runnable will return null */
    final Object result1 = future1.get();
    log("The result from the runnable is: '" + result1 + '\'');

    final Object result2 = future2.get();
    log("The result from the callable is: '" + result2 + '\'');

    final Object result3 = future3.get();
    log("The result from the runnable+result is: '" + result3 + '\'');

    try {
        future4.get(3, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        log("Task 4 completed in time");
    } catch (final TimeoutException e) {
        log("Task 4 timed out; the task is still running");
        final boolean cancelled = future4.cancel(true);
        log("Requested cancellation of task 4: " + cancelled);
    }

    log("The first three futures completed");
}
```

The Java Memory Model connection is the
[`ExecutorService` memory-consistency guarantee](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ExecutorService.html):
actions before submitting a task happen-before its actions, which in turn
happen-before a successful `Future.get()` return. This makes data handed into a
task, and its completed result, visible across the hand-off. It does not
guarantee task start or completion order, cancellation, fairness, or atomicity
of compound actions.

### 2. Recurring maintenance work

Periodic work has no natural completion, so the example schedules a fixed-rate
task and cancels it explicitly. This is appropriate only when the task’s
runtime, failure behaviour, and shutdown policy are understood.

### 3. Many blocking file operations

Hashing each file is independent and spends most of its time in file I/O. A
virtual-thread-per-task executor lets the example submit one blocking task per
file without treating the number of platform worker threads as the limit.

```java
    } catch (final IOException e) {
        throw new UncheckedIOException("Failed to walk directory", e);
    }

    /* Wait for all tasks to complete */
    for (final Future<?> future : futures) {
        future.get();
    }
    log("All file hashes computed.");
}


logSection("Execute Multiple Tasks (invokeAll())");

```

### 4. A batch with all results required

`invokeAll()` submits the batch and blocks until every task completes. The
returned futures retain the input order, not completion order. It is a poor fit
when the caller should process early results or fail fast.

```java
                return "Task B";
            },
            () -> {
                sleepForAFewSeconds();
                return "Task C";
            });

    log("Invoke all tasks");
    final List<Future<String>> results = executor.invokeAll(tasks);
    for (final Future<String> result : results) {
        log("Task completed with result: " + result.get());
    }
}
}

private static void computeSha256(final Path file) {
try {
    final MessageDigest digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
    try (DigestInputStream dis = new DigestInputStream(new BufferedInputStream(Files.newInputStream(file)), digest)) {
        final byte[] buffer = new byte[8192];
        while (dis.read(buffer) != -1) ; /* Process file in chunks */
    }
    final String hashHex = HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest.digest());
```

### Choosing an API

- Use an `ExecutorService` when code needs an explicit execution policy,
  lifecycle control, or a `Future` for an independently submitted task.
- Use `ScheduledExecutorService` for delayed or periodic work. Periodic tasks
  need explicit cancellation and a defined shutdown policy.

A fixed thread pool limits concurrent workers, but its queued tasks still need
a capacity and overload policy in a real application. Virtual threads reduce
the cost of blocking tasks; they do not make database connections, HTTP calls,
or other external resources unlimited.
